steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a computer vision paper on a bidirectional temporal diffusion model that generates temporally consistent human animations. Explain the problem with existing generative and auto-regressive approaches, our bidirectional idea and how we implement it with diffusion, what the experiments show, and list the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Problem: generative models handle appearance but not time; our goal and applications
- Why unidirectional auto-regression drifts
- Our idea: bidirectional modeling
- Realization with a denoising diffusion model
- Experimental findings
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Problem and goal
  - humans express space-time continuum via appearance + motion
  - existing generative models restore space (high-quality images, diverse appearance) but fail on time (temporally incoherent motion)
  - our method: temporal modeling of generative network -> temporally consistent human animations
  - three input modalities: random noise, single image, single video (Figure 1)
  - applications: novel content creation for non-expert media artists; pre-visualization refined by professional video creators
- Unidirectional auto-regression
  - temporal modeling often = video auto-regression: past frames condition future frames
  - forward auto-regression smooth but texture drifting, e.g. skirt texture distorted along movements (Figure 2)
  - cause: motion-appearance ambiguity - infinite possible future appearances even for same motion -> artifacts (e.g. distortion) amplified over time
- Bidirectional modeling
  - decode appearance in context of both forward and backward image regression, intermediate features cross-conditioned over time
  - key observation: bidirectional temporal consistency in feature space suppresses ambiguity -> no texture drifting, keeps temporal smoothness
- Realization with diffusion
  - generative denoising diffusion model
  - denoising network iteratively removes temporal Gaussian noise, guided by conditioning poses + appearance style
  - inspired by message passing in dynamic programming: recursively cross-condition intermediate results between consecutive frames bidirectionally (Figure 3)
  - locally consistent for consecutive frames at first denoising step, progressively refined each iteration -> globally coherent over all frames
- Findings
  - from a single image: strong temporal coherence, beats unidirectional generative models
  - learning from multiple frames (person-specific video) further improves physical plausibility
  - generates diverse clothing styles and identities without conditioning images
- Contributions
  - (1) bidirectional temporal diffusion model; from random noise, single image or video
  - (2) feature cross-conditioning between consecutive frames w/ recursive sampling; motion context in denoising, locally + globally consistent
  - (3) quantitative + qualitative: strong temporal coherence vs. unidirectional methods; new high-quality synthetic data via graphics simulation -> ground truth (different people, perfectly same motion)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Humans express their own space-time continuum through appearance and motion. Existing generative models have been successful at restoring the space, i.e., generating high-quality images with diverse human appearance, but they often fail to decode the time, e.g., the human motion is temporally incoherent. In this paper we introduce a method for temporal modeling of a generative network so that it can synthesize temporally consistent human animations. Our method can generate a human animation from three different modalities, which are a random noise, a single image, and a single video, as shown in Figure. 1. These generated human animations make a number of applications possible, including creating novel content for media artists who are not experts, and pre-visualization of human animation which professional video creators can then refine.

Temporal modeling for human animation has often been formulated as a video auto-regression problem, where past frames are used as a condition to decode future frames. This kind of unidirectional generation (forward auto-regression) has shown smooth animation results, but it often has the problem of texture drifting, e.g., the texture on a person's clothing like the skirt in Figure 2 gets largely distorted along its dynamic movements. The main reason for this is the significant motion-appearance ambiguity: there are infinite solutions for the future state of the human appearance even with the same motion, and this amplifies the artifacts (e.g., distortion) over time.

To suppress this motion-appearance ambiguity, we model the human appearance bidirectionally. A generative network decodes the human appearance in the context of both forward and backward image regression, and the intermediate features are cross-conditioned over time. Our key observation is that bidirectional temporal consistency in the feature space strongly suppresses the motion-appearance ambiguity, and this prevents the texture drifting while keeping the temporal smoothness.

- Realization with diffusion
  - generative denoising diffusion model
  - denoising network iteratively removes temporal Gaussian noises, guided by conditioning poses + appearance style
  - inspired by message passing in dynamic programming -> recursive bidirectional cross-conditioning of intermediate results between consecutive frames (Figure 3)
  - first denoising step: locally consistent for consecutive frames; refined each iteration -> globally coherent for entire frames
- Findings
  - single image -> strong temporal coherence, outperforms unidirectional generative models
  - person-specific video (multiple frames) -> better physical plausibility
  - diverse clothing styles + identities without conditioning images
- Contributions
  - (1) bidirectional temporal diffusion model: random noise, single image, or video
  - (2) feature cross-conditioning w/ recursive sampling (dynamic message passing) -> motion context embedded locally + globally consistently
  - (3) quantitative + qualitative temporal coherence vs. unidirectional methods; new synthetic data via graphics simulation for ground truth (different people, perfectly same motion)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Humans express their own space-time continuum through appearance and motion. Existing generative models have been successful at restoring the space, i.e., generating high-quality images with diverse human appearance, but they often fail to decode the time, e.g., the human motion is temporally incoherent. In this paper we introduce a method for temporal modeling of a generative network so that it can synthesize temporally consistent human animations. Our method can generate a human animation from three different modalities, which are a random noise, a single image, and a single video, as shown in Figure. 1. These generated human animations make a number of applications possible, including creating novel content for media artists who are not experts, and pre-visualization of human animation which professional video creators can then refine.

Temporal modeling for human animation has often been formulated as a video auto-regression problem, where past frames are used as a condition to decode future frames. This kind of unidirectional generation (forward auto-regression) has shown smooth animation results, but it often has the problem of texture drifting, e.g., the texture on a person's clothing like the skirt in Figure 2 gets largely distorted along its dynamic movements. The main reason for this is the significant motion-appearance ambiguity: there are infinite solutions for the future state of the human appearance even with the same motion, and this amplifies the artifacts (e.g., distortion) over time.

To suppress this motion-appearance ambiguity, we model the human appearance bidirectionally. A generative network decodes the human appearance in the context of both forward and backward image regression, and the intermediate features are cross-conditioned over time. Our key observation is that bidirectional temporal consistency in the feature space strongly suppresses the motion-appearance ambiguity, and this prevents the texture drifting while keeping the temporal smoothness.

We implement the idea of bidirectional temporal modeling with a generative denoising diffusion model. A denoising network learns to remove temporal Gaussian noises iteratively in order to generate the human animation, guided by the conditioning poses and the appearance style. Inspired by message passing algorithms in dynamic programming, we recursively cross-condition the intermediate results between consecutive frames in a bidirectional way, as shown in Figure 3. At the first denoising step the temporal context of the human appearance is locally consistent for consecutive frames, and then it is progressively refined at every denoising iteration so that it becomes globally coherent for the entire frames.

In the experiments, we show that our bidirectional denoising diffusion model generates human animations from a single image with strong temporal coherence, and it outperforms the results of unidirectional generative models. We also show that learning from multiple frames, i.e., a video of a specific person, can improve the physical plausibility of the generated human animation even more. Finally, we show that our method can generate human animations with diverse clothing styles and identities without any conditioning images.

Contribution (1) We propose a bidirectional temporal diffusion model that can generate temporally coherent human animation from random noise, a single image, or a video. (2) We introduce feature cross-conditioning between consecutive frames with recursive sampling, inspired by dynamic message passing algorithms, and this lets us embed the motion context in the iterative denoising process in a way that is locally and globally consistent. (3) We show quantitatively and qualitatively that our method has strong temporal coherence compared to existing unidirectional methods. For an accurate evaluation we create new high-quality synthetic data of people in dynamic movements using graphics simulation, which gives ground-truth data, i.e., different people in the perfectly same motion.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Humans express their own space-time continuum in the form of appearance and motion. While existing generative models [1,2] have succeeded in restoring the space, i.e., high-quality image generation with diverse human appearance, they often fail to decode the time, e.g., producing temporally incoherent human motion. In this paper, we introduce a method for temporal modeling of a generative network to synthesize temporally consistent human animations. Our method can generate a human animation from three different modalities, a random noise, a single image, and a single video, as shown in Figure. 1. Such generated human animations enable a number of applications, including novel content creation for non-expert media artists and pre-visualization of human animation that can be further refined by professional video creators.

Temporal modeling for human animation has often been formulated as a video auto-regression problem, using past frames as a condition to decode future frames. While such unidirectional generation (forward auto-regression) has shown smooth animation results, it often suffers from texture drifting, e.g., the texture on a person's clothing, such as the skirt in Figure 2, is largely distorted along its dynamic movements. This is mainly due to the significant motion-appearance ambiguity, where infinite solutions exist for the future state of human appearance even with the same motion, which amplifies the artifacts (e.g., distortion) over time.

To suppress this motion-appearance ambiguity, we model human appearance bidirectionally: a generative network decodes the human appearance in the context of both forward and backward image regression, with intermediate features cross-conditioned over time. Our key observation is that bidirectional temporal consistency in feature space strongly suppresses the motion-appearance ambiguity, which prevents texture drifting while maintaining temporal smoothness.

We realize bidirectional temporal modeling using a generative denoising diffusion model [3]. A denoising network learns to iteratively remove temporal Gaussian noises to generate the human animation, guided by conditioning poses and appearance style. Inspired by message passing algorithms in dynamic programming [4,5], we recursively cross-condition the intermediate results between consecutive frames in a bidirectional way, as shown in Figure 3; the temporal context of human appearance is locally consistent for consecutive frames at the first denoising step and is progressively refined at every denoising iteration to become globally coherent for the entire frames.

In the experiments, we demonstrate that our bidirectional denoising diffusion model generates human animations from a single image with strong temporal coherence, outperforming unidirectional generative models. We also show that learning from multiple frames, i.e., a person-specific video, further improves the physical plausibility of the generated human animation. Finally, we showcase that our method can generate human animations with diverse clothing styles and identities without any conditioning images.

Contribution (1) We propose a bidirectional temporal diffusion model that generates temporally coherent human animation from random noise, a single image, or a video. (2) Inspired by dynamic message passing algorithms, we introduce feature cross-conditioning between consecutive frames with recursive sampling, which embeds the motion context in the iterative denoising process in a locally and globally consistent way. (3) We demonstrate quantitatively and qualitatively that our method shows strong temporal coherence compared to existing unidirectional methods. For accurate evaluation, we create new high-quality synthetic data of people in dynamic movements using graphics simulation, which provides ground-truth data, i.e., different people in the perfectly same motion.
